title: Perceptual Evaluations: Evals for Aesthetics — Diego Rodriguez, Krea.ai

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is the inadequacy of current evaluation metrics like FID and CLIP for assessing generative media aesthetics, and it proposes opinion-trained continuous classifiers as a new evaluation methodology.

summary: Diego Rodriguez, co-founder of Krea.ai (a generative media startup), presents a talk on perceptual evaluations—evals that account for human perception, opinion, and aesthetics. He opens with a striking example: when asked to evaluate an obviously unnatural AI-generated hand, o3 (despite tool-calling, Python analysis, and OpenCV) concluded it was 'mostly natural,' revealing that even systems claimed to approach AGI cannot make simple perceptual judgments humans perform instinctively. He notes AI models are trained on human data, human preference data, and data limited by human preconceived notions and perception. Rodriguez provides historical context through Claude Shannon's information theory, originally focused on communication. He draws parallels between Shannon's source-channel-receiver model and neural network architectures like variational autoencoders. He then explains how compression formats—JPEG, MP3, MP4—all exploit human perceptual limitations: JPEG downsamples color channels because humans are insensitive to color detail relative to brightness, achieving roughly 50% data reduction while appearing identical. He reflects on studying artificial systems engineering, where deleting information from images produced no perceptible difference. This raises a critical concern: if AI training data comes from the compressed internet, models may inherit a 'contagion' of human perceptual flaws. He illustrates with Clean FID research showing FID scores degrade dramatically under JPEG artifacts even though images are perceptually identical, questioning why such metrics decide whether generative models are good or bad. Current metrics measure easy attributes (object count, color adherence via CLIP) but miss aesthetics, artistic meaning, and subjective qualities. Rodriguez cites a Midjourney colleague's analogy: predicting the car was easy, but predicting traffic was hard—what 'traffic' equivalents are we missing? He invokes the Tower of Babel myth, noting AI has now solved translation, enabling communication across languages without shared fluency. In the Q&A, he proposes training continuous classifiers on human opinion: showing a classifier sets of good images that may contain various artifact types, letting it learn the 'you know it when you see it' judgment that AI excels at. He concludes with a brief Krea company slide and a hiring call for aesthetics research, hyperpersonalization, and real-time generative AI scaling across image, video, audio, and 3D.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Perceptual Evaluations
sections.summary: Diego Rodriguez introduces himself as co-founder of Krea.ai and frames the talk around evaluating AI when human perception, opinion, and aesthetics must be considered.

sections.title: The Problem with Current AI Evaluations
sections.summary: Rodriguez shows an AI-generated hand that obviously looks unnatural, but when o3 evaluates it using tool-calling and OpenCV over 17 seconds, it concludes the hand is 'mostly natural.' He notes AI models are trained on human data, human preference data, and data limited by human perception, raising the question of what we can do better.

sections.title: Historical Context and Compression
sections.summary: Rodriguez traces evaluation thinking to Claude Shannon's information theory, originally about communication. He explains how JPEG exploits human insensitivity to color detail versus brightness, achieving roughly 50% data reduction with no perceptible difference. The same principle yields MP3 for audio and MP4 for video. He reflects on his artificial systems engineering background where deleting image information produced no visible difference.

sections.title: Limitations in AI and Human-centric Metrics
sections.summary: Rodriguez warns that AI training data from the compressed internet creates a 'contagion' of human perceptual flaws into models. He shows Clean FID research where FID scores degrade dramatically under JPEG artifacts despite perceptually identical images, questioning why such metrics decide generative model quality. Current metrics measure easy attributes (object count, color via CLIP) but miss aesthetics, artistic meaning, and subjective qualities.

sections.title: Rethinking Evaluation and the Future of AI
sections.summary: Rodriguez cites a Midjourney colleague's analogy: predicting the car was easy, but predicting traffic was hard—what 'traffic' equivalents are we missing? He invokes the Tower of Babel myth and notes AI has now solved translation, enabling cross-lingual communication without shared fluency (he provides Japanese customer support without speaking Japanese). This should inform how evaluations evolve to incorporate human opinion and perception.

sections.title: Evaluating Our Evaluations
sections.summary: Rodriguez argues evaluations should account for human opinion, visual learning styles, and training data artifacts. Evals should consider whether a blue is the right blue and whether meaning conveyed in an image is accessible only to humans.

sections.title: Krea's Role and Call to Action
sections.summary: Rodriguez briefly presents Krea's growth from 8 to 12 people and announces hiring for aesthetics research, hyperpersonalization, and real-time generative AI scaling. Q&A begins with a question about perceptually-aware metrics, which he notes exist in traditional encoding but urges broader adoption and training of classifiers.

sections.title: Q&A: Training Continuous Classifiers on Opinion
sections.summary: Rodriguez proposes training continuous classifiers on human opinion by showing sets of good images that may contain various artifact types beyond JPEG. He frames this as the type of 'you know it when you see it' question where machine learning excels, since it is fundamentally about opinions rather than objective metrics.
